subject: English
passage: Archaeologist Usman Vo and colleagues have reported the discovery at a quarry in Yorkshire of several intact crucibles, fragments of blown vessels, and vitrified furnace debris from the late second century CE. The researchers have concluded that the area once housed a working glassblowers' workshop, a specialized branch of Romano-British industrial sites. The finding is significant given the previous absence of known glass-production workshops in northern regions of Roman Britain, which had led many scholars to assume that finished glassware was transported north from southern manufacturing centers.
prompt: What does the text most strongly suggest about the site discovered by the researchers?

choices.A: It is the earliest known example of a Romano-British glassblowers' workshop.
choices.B: It was particularly challenging to excavate because it was located within an active quarry.
choices.C: It may have housed other types of Romano-British industrial activity in addition to glassblowing.
choices.D: It is farther north than any other glass-production workshop discovered in Roman Britain.

explanation:
Choice D is the best answer because it presents a statement supported by the text. The passage describes Vo and colleagues' discovery of crucibles, vessel fragments, and furnace debris in a Yorkshire quarry, which led the researchers to conclude that the location once housed a glassblowers' workshop. The text then notes that this finding is significant because of the 'previous absence of known glass-production workshops in northern regions of Roman Britain.' If no other glass-production workshops have been found in northern Roman Britain and this Yorkshire site is the first, then the text strongly suggests that the site lies farther north than any other such workshop discovered in Roman Britain.

Why A is incorrect:

Choice A is incorrect because the text does not suggest that the Yorkshire site is the oldest known Romano-British glassblowers' workshop, only that it is the first such workshop found in the northern regions of Roman Britain. The text offers no comparison between the age of this site and the ages of other known glass-production workshops.
